History of Present Illness:
This is a ___ yo M with a PMH significant for obesity, HTN, 
Hyperlipidemia, DM2, and tobacco abuse who presented to the 
hospital with 3 days of chest pressure and a recent ECHO that 
showed an EF ___. The patient describes the chest pressure as 
in a band like distribution on the ___ the sternum without 
radiation to his arm or back. The patient says that this pain 
came on at rest without exertion and was not associated with 
nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, nor was it exacerbated by deep 
breaths or position. The patient does note that eating makes the 
pressure feel tighter and more full. Of note, the patient 
describes months-years of chest pain with exertion. He says that 
he had to give up his weight loss regimen a few months back due 
to what he describes as crescendo angina. The patient had never 
had chest pain at rest until this most recent episode. Of note, 
the patient had c/o chronic dyspnea to his PCP. He recently had 
a TTE that showed severe ischemic cardiomyopathy. The patient 
notes long-standing DOE, 3-pillow orthopnea, PND, and some ___ 
swelling.
.
The patient attributed many of these symptoms to a hiatal hernia 
that was diagnosed in the past. He does note significant 
indigestion and heart burn symptoms.  
.  
In the ED, the patient was given aspirin, SL nitro x 2, 
metoprolol, and IV lasix. An EKG did not show active signs of 
ischemia. The patient was started on a heparin gtt for unstable 
angina and transfered to the floor for further management.   
.  
On arrival to the floor, patient has no new complaints. 
.  
REVIEW OF SYSTEMS  
On review of systems, he denies any prior history of stroke, 
TIA, deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, bleeding at the 
time of surgery, myalgias, joint pains, cough, hemoptysis, black 
stools or red stools. he denies recent fevers, chills or rigors. 
he denies exertional buttock or calf pain. All of the other 
review of systems were negative.

TTE from outpatient in early ___:
1. Mildly dilated LV. There is mild concentric left ventricular 
hypertrophy. The posterior and inferior walls are severely 
hypokinetic to akinetic, the distal half of the inferior septum 
is moderately hypokinetic, the distal lateral wall is moderately 
hypokinetic, the rest of the lateral wall is mildly hypokinetic. 
 and the apex is severely hypokinetic.  The anterior septum has 
the best movement but it, too, is mildly hypokinetic. The LVEF 
is severely reduced, in the range of probably only 20%. No LV 
clot is seen. The mean E' velocity is low at < 7 cm/sec. The 
E/E' ratios were 10 and 18, the 18 suggesting elevation of the 
LVEDP. Restrictive filling is also present by deceleration time 
of < 105 msec.
2. The left atrial volume is severely increased.
3. The right ventricle is  not optimally seen for size or 
funcction on the apical views. On the subcostal view, the RV 
appears sig hypokinetic.
4. There is mild aortic regurgitation.
5. There is no evidence of aortic stenosis. The systolic 
velocity is low at 0.83-0.93 m/sec, suggesting reduced forward 
stroke volume.
6. There is mild mitral regurgitation.
7. The aortic root, measured at the level of the sinuses of 
Valsalva,  is of normal caliber 3.9 cm for BSA.
8. The ascending aorta and transverse aorta are dilated
measuring 4.2 and 3.7 cm, respectively.
9. No prior report available for comparison. Dr ___ was 
notified of the severe LV dysfunction, with regional variation 
suggesting a severe ischemic cardiomyopathy.   
 
Brief Hospital Course:
This is a ___ yo M with poorly controlled DM2 (HgbA1c 11.2%), 
HTN, HL, and obesity who presents with 3 days of chest pain at 
rest and a recent diagnosis of ischemic systolic heart failure. 
.  
1. Unstable Angina: The patient's chest pain was slightly 
atypical in distribution and quality making it difficult to 
discern cardiac from GI. The patient, however, had multiple risk 
factors for CAD, new heart failure, and more prominent q waves 
on EKG. The patient underwent a R and L heart cath that showed a 
single vessel (LCx) 60% lesion. No intervention was undertaken. 
The patient will need optimal medical management of his multiple 
risk factors including HTN, HL, and DM2. The patient was 
discharged on aspirin, metoprolol, lisinopril, and atorvastatin.
.  
2. Acute on Chronic Ischemic Systolic Heart Failure 
Exacerbation: The patient had a recent TTE showing an EF ___ 
and hypokinesis and akineses in a multi-vessle distribution. 
This is likely ischemic cardiomyopathy, but the chronicity and 
reversibility is unclear. Pt with LCx disease as above, and also 
found to have PCWP 19. The patient was given low doses of IV 
lasix with good urine output, however, he will need optimization 
as an outpatient. The patient will continue metoprolol, 
lisinopril, lasix, and spironolactone and this will be 
uptitrated as an outpatient.
.  
3. HTN: Medical treatment with metoprolol, lisinopril, lasix.  
.  
4. HL: Atorvastatin
.  
5. DM2: Metformin and Glargine at home dose.
.

- Restart metformin after ensuring good GFR

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

It was a pleasure caring for you at the hospital. 
.
You were admitted to the hospital with new heart failure and 
chest pain. You received a catheterization which revealed 1 
tight blockage of a heart artery. It was felt your symptoms were 
not being caused by this blocked artery and no intervention was 
done. You were started on several medications which will help to 
treat your heart failure and to prevent any further damage to 
your heart. You will have to follow up with your doctors as ___ 
outpatient to have these medication doses changed further. 
.
Please follow up with the appointments below. 
.

START Furosemide (Lasix) 40mg daily
START Lisinopril 10 mg by mouth daily 
START Metoprolol Succinate 50mg by mouth daily 
START Atorvastatin 80my by mouth daily 
START Spironolactone 25mg by mouth daily 
START Omeprazole 20mg by mouth twice daily
STOP Simvastatin 
STOP Triamterene-HCTZ
Continue your insulin dosing (Lantus) 
Continue your baby aspirin 
Do not restart your Metformin until you see your primary care 
doctor next week for ___ when your electrolytes can be 
rechecked. This can likely be restarted then. 
.
You will need to see your primary care physician next week for 
repeat laboratory testing to assess your kidney function.

important to monitor your electrolytes, potassium in particular, 
and kidney function (creatinine).
